answers.answer:
Summary: SCOP/SCOPe places the bulge domain of the A subunit of the A-type/V-type (V1) ATP synthase in the all-beta class (b), in the barrel-sandwich hybrid fold b.84, but as its own superfamily rather than inside the Single hybrid motif (b.84.1), Rudiment single hybrid motif (b.84.2) or Duplicated hybrid motif (b.84.3) superfamilies. The classic domain is the ~90-residue insertion in the Pyrococcus horikoshii A subunit structure (PDB 1vdz, later A-subunit structures such as 3i4l/3i72), added around SCOP 1.73 and carried through SCOPe 2.0x. The separate-superfamily placement is a statement that the bulge shares architecture and topology with the other hybrid-motif domains, but that SCOP finds no evidence of common ancestry with them.

Why a shared fold but a separate superfamily:
- The SCOP fold level only asserts that domains have the same major secondary structures in the same arrangement with the same topology; the barrel-sandwich hybrid is described as a sandwich of half-barrel-shaped beta-sheets. The bulge domain satisfies this geometric criterion.
- The superfamily level requires probable common evolutionary origin, inferred from structural similarity plus sequence motifs, conserved functional residues, shared ligands or binding modes, or shared genomic/domain context. None of these link the bulge to the other b.84 superfamilies. b.84.1 contains biotinyl/lipoyl carrier domains that present a lysine-linked swinging-arm cofactor; b.84.2 contains the C-terminal rudiment domains of ATP-grasp enzymes such as biotin carboxylase and carbamoyl phosphate synthetase; b.84.3 contains the internally duplicated zinc metallopeptidase M23 (LytM/lysostaphin) catalytic domain. The bulge has no detectable sequence similarity to any of these, no cofactor-attachment lysine, no metal site and no peptidase activity.
- The bulge arises in a completely different protein context: it is an insertion within the N-terminal beta-barrel domain of the A subunit, a domain that SCOP classifies with the F1 alpha/beta subunit N-terminal domains (fold b.49), while the catalytic core is a RecA-like P-loop NTPase domain (c.37.1) and the C-terminal domain is all-alpha (a.69.1). The insertion is absent from the homologous F1 beta subunit, so it was acquired independently within the rotary ATPase lineage, not inherited from any hybrid-motif protein. Its proposed role is structural, mediating contacts with the stator/peripheral stalk or modulating the nucleotide-binding region, which again gives no functional handle to tie it to biotinyl/lipoyl carriers or peptidases.

The evolutionary claim and its limits:
- The placement asserts analogy, not homology, between the bulge and the other hybrid-motif superfamilies. SCOP is explicit that domains in the same fold but different superfamilies may have arrived at the same topology by convergence or by physical preference for a favored fold, and that the hierarchy deliberately does not claim they descend from a common ancestor. It is a conservative, negative statement: homology cannot be demonstrated, so it is not asserted. It does not positively claim convergence either; a very remote common origin is simply not supported by available evidence.
- Within the superfamily, the claim is homology only among A-subunit bulge domains across archaeal A-ATPases and eukaryotic V-ATPase A subunits, which is well supported by sequence conservation of the whole A subunit.

Practical consequences for homology, function transfer, template use and representatives:
- Do not transfer function across b.84 superfamilies: the bulge should not be annotated as a biotin/lipoyl attachment domain, an ATP-grasp accessory domain or an M23 peptidase, and conversely those families should not be assigned a stator-contact role.
- Fold-level template use is limited to general topology; the other hybrid-motif structures are acceptable only as remote structural analogs for secondary-structure arrangement, not for placing functional residues or ligands, and sequence-based threading alignments between superfamilies are not reliable.
- The bulge superfamily is essentially monotypic in SCOPe, with representatives drawn from a handful of A-subunit structures of the same protein, so superfamily-level statistics such as structural variability or sequence divergence are not meaningful, and representative selection cannot be used to argue for or against relationships to the other b.84 superfamilies.
- Any future reclassification merging the bulge with another hybrid-motif superfamily would require new evidence of the kind SCOP uses at the superfamily level: detectable sequence similarity (for example profile-profile or HMM hits of significant score), shared functionally constrained residues, or shared ligand/partner binding mode, none of which currently exists. Note also that SCOPe largely freezes manual superfamily assignments from SCOP 1.75, so the separate placement reflects the evidence available at that time; other hierarchies such as ECOD may treat such fold-level relationships differently and should not be assumed to agree.
